children: Lending to eurozone businesses halved in August, a sign that rising borrowing costs following the European Central Bank's decision to raise its key interest rate are hindering investment.
The ECB on Friday said that bank loans to businesses totaled 11 billion euros ($12.52 billion) during the month, down from 22 billion euros in July and 27 billion euros in June.

The central bank raised its key interest rate to 2.25% from 2% in June, responding to a pickup in the annual rate of inflation as the U.S.-Iran war pushed energy prices higher. Earlier this month, it raised its key interest rate to 2.5%.
The sharp decline in bank lending to businesses since May suggests the tightening in monetary policy is having some impact on economic activity, and particularly on investment.
Eurozone businesses rely more heavily on bank lending to fund investment than their counterparts in the U.S., where the bond markets play a larger role.
According to the ECB's figures, loans to businesses with a maturity of more than five years fell to 8 billion euros in August from 21 billion euros in June.
As a result of the slowdown over recent months, the annual rate of growth of business loans fell to 4.2% in August from 4.4% in July.

The ECB's figures showed that lending to households rose to 19 billion euros from 17 billion euros in July, including a slight increase in mortgage loans. The annual rate of growth was unchanged at 3.1%.

The eurozone economy has shown surprising resilience in the face of the higher energy prices caused by the U.S.-Iran war. However, investment has been a weak spot, declining slightly in each of the first two quarters.

The ECB views 2.5% as the upper end of the range in which its key interest rate is neither stimulating nor restraining activity. Investors expect the central bank to push into restrictive territory by the end of this year.
